ai.literal: In the place where it prevails, he who restrains, anger restrains; in the place where it does not prevail, if one restrains what? if one does not restrain what?
ai.translation: He who restrains his anger where it can have effect is the one who truly restrains it. Where it has no effect, what does it matter whether he restrains it or not?
ai.modern: தன் கோபம் செல்லுபடியாகும் இடத்தில் அதைக் கட்டுப்படுத்துபவனே கோபத்தைக் காப்பவன் ஆவான்; செல்லுபடியாகாத இடத்தில் அதைக் கட்டுப்படுத்தினால் என்ன, கட்டுப்படுத்தாவிட்டால் என்ன?
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the true nature of anger management. Restraining anger is meaningful only when one has the power to express it and cause harm, such as towards subordinates or those who are weaker. In situations where one's anger has no power or effect, such as towards superiors or those who are stronger, it makes no difference whether one restrains it or lets it flare up, as it cannot affect the other person anyway. Therefore, true self-control is demonstrated only when one chooses not to be angry despite having the power to enforce it.

ai.literal: In the place where it does not work, anger is bad; even in the place where it works, there are no other things more evil than that.
ai.translation: Anger is harmful when directed at those where it has no effect; even when directed at those where it does have an effect, there is nothing more evil than it.
ai.modern: தன் கோபம் செல்லுபடியாகாத இடத்தில் கோபம் கொள்வது தீமையானது; தன் கோபம் செல்லுபடியாகும் இடத்திலும் அதைவிடத் தீமையானது வேறு எதுவும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet analyzes the consequences of anger in two distinct situations: against those who are stronger and against those who are weaker. In a situation where one's anger cannot prevail (against the powerful), harboring anger only causes self-harm and distress. Conversely, in a situation where one's anger does prevail (against the powerless), exercising it is the ultimate evil because it leads to oppression and moral ruin. Therefore, anger is entirely destructive and unjustifiable in any circumstance.

ai.literal: Forgetting anger towards anyone; evil things arising because of that will come.
ai.translation: One should forget anger towards anyone whomsoever, for all evil things arise because of it.
ai.modern: யாரிடத்திலும் கோபம் கொள்வதை மறந்துவிட வேண்டும்; ஏனென்றால், தீமைகள் அனைத்தும் அந்தக் கோபத்தினாலேயே உண்டாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains why we must completely avoid anger. The word 'மறத்தல்' literally means forgetting, but here it carries the sense of completely letting go or abandoning. We must do this 'யார்மாட்டும்'—towards anyone, regardless of their status or how they treat us. The second line warns that 'தீய' (evil consequences and pain) will 'பிறத்தல்' (arise) 'அதனான்' (because of that anger). Thus, by showing that anger is the sole source of harmful outcomes, the poet urges us to eliminate it entirely.

ai.literal: Smile and joy which destroys, than anger, enemy are there other?
ai.translation: Is there any other enemy greater than anger, which destroys both one's outward smile and inward joy?
ai.modern: முகத்தில் தோன்றும் நகையையும் மனதில் தோன்றும் மகிழ்ச்சியையும் அழிக்கும் கோபத்தை விட வேறு கொடிய பகை உண்டோ?
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the destructive nature of anger by comparing it to an enemy. Anger is the ultimate enemy because it destroys two of a person's most precious qualities: their outward smile (நகை) and their inward joy (உவகை). The rhetorical question 'are there other enemies?' emphasizes that no external adversary can cause as much self-harm as one's own anger.

ai.literal: If oneself indeed protects, anger let one restrain; if not restrained, oneself indeed will destroy, anger.
ai.translation: If you wish to protect yourself, restrain your anger; if you do not restrain it, that very anger will destroy you.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் தன்னைத் தான் காத்துக் கொள்ள விரும்பினால், தன் கோபத்தைக் கட்டுப்படுத்திக் காக்க வேண்டும்; அவ்வாறு காக்காவிட்டால், அந்தக் கோபமே அவனை அழித்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the self-destructive nature of anger. The author advises that if a person wishes to protect their own well-being, the primary thing they must guard against is their own anger ('cinam'). The conditional 'kākkiṉ' (if one protects) is paired with the imperative 'kākka' (let one restrain), emphasizing that self-preservation is directly tied to anger management. If one fails to do so ('kāvākkāl'), the anger does not just harm others; it turns inward and destroys ('kollum') the very person ('taṉṉaiyē') who harbors it.

ai.literal: Anger, which is called the killer of those who associate with it, will burn the protective raft called kinship.
ai.translation: Anger, the fire that destroys those who harbor it, will burn down the protective raft of one's family and friends.
ai.modern: தன்னைச் சேர்ந்தவர்களையே அழிக்கும் நெருப்பாகிய சினம், ஒருவருக்குப் பாதுகாப்பாக இருக்கும் சுற்றம் என்னும் தெப்பத்தையும் எரித்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a powerful metaphor to warn against anger. It describes anger as 'சேர்ந்தாரைக் கொல்லி'—a fire that destroys the very person who harbors it. Furthermore, this destructive fire does not stop there; it spreads to burn down 'இனம் என்னும் ஏமப்புணை', which is the protective raft of one's relatives and friends. Just as a raft saves a person from drowning in a stormy sea, one's kin protect them from life's hardships, but anger completely destroys this vital support system.

ai.literal: The ruin of him who holds anger as a valuable thing is like the hand of him who struck the ground not failing to hurt.
ai.translation: The ruin of one who cherishes anger as a valuable thing is as certain and unavoidable as the pain felt in the hand of someone who strikes the ground.
ai.modern: கோபத்தை ஒரு சிறந்த குணமாகக் கொண்டு அதை வளர்ப்பவனுடைய அழிவானது, தரையைத் தன் கையால் அடித்தவனுடைய கைக்கு வலி ஏற்படுவது தப்பாது என்பதைப் போன்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet illustrates the self-destructive nature of anger using a vivid, everyday physical analogy. The poet compares harboring anger to striking the ground with one's bare hand. Just as the ground remains unharmed while the hand that strikes it inevitably suffers pain, the person who holds onto anger only ends up destroying themselves rather than hurting the object of their anger. The key word 'பொருள்' (meaning a valuable asset or reality) shows how foolish it is to treat a destructive emotion like anger as something worth holding onto.

ai.literal: Even if one does painful things like the touch of a cluster of fire, if possible, not getting angry is good.
ai.translation: Even if someone inflicts painful harms as agonizing as being touched by a blazing fire, it is best, if one can manage it, to refrain from anger.
ai.modern: நெருப்புக் கூட்டத்தைத் தொடுவது போன்ற துன்பங்களை ஒருவன் நமக்குச் செய்தாலும், முடிந்தவரை அவனிடம் கோபம் கொள்ளாமல் இருப்பது நல்லது.
ai.explanation: The couplet highlights the supreme value of patience and anger management under extreme provocation. The poet compares severe, malicious harm to the physical agony of being touched by a blazing, multi-tongued fire ('இணர் எரி'). Even when subjected to such intense pain, the author advises that if one can possibly summon the strength ('புணரின்'), remaining free from anger ('வெகுளாமை') is the best course of action. This emphasizes that self-control is not just for minor annoyances but is most crucial and noble during the most severe trials.

ai.literal: That which is thought of all immediately will attain, if with the mind one does not harbor anger.
ai.translation: If a person does not harbor anger even in their mind, they will immediately attain everything they think of.
ai.modern: ஒருவர் தன் மனதால் கோபத்தை நினைக்காமல் இருந்தால், அவர் நினைத்தவை அனைத்தும் உடனே அவரை வந்தடையும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the immense mental power and clarity gained by conquering anger. The poet states that if a person completely avoids harboring anger within their mind, they gain such focus that whatever they desire or think of will be attained immediately. The repetition of the root word for mind and thought emphasizes that true self-control begins in the deep recesses of the mind. By keeping the mind free from the destructive heat of anger, one's thoughts gain the strength to manifest instantly.

ai.literal: Those who transgressed are like those who died; those who gave up anger are equal to those who renounced.
ai.translation: Those who transgress limits through anger are like those who are dead; those who give up anger are equal to the ascetics who have renounced the world.
ai.modern: சினம்கொண்டு வரம்பு மீறியவர்கள் இறந்தவர்களுக்கு ஒப்பாவார்கள்; சினத்தைத் துறந்தவர்கள் உலகப்பற்றைத் துறந்த முனிவர்களுக்கு ஒப்பாவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a powerful parallel structure to contrast those who yield to anger with those who conquer it. The poet states that people who lose control and transgress the bounds of virtue through anger are as good as dead, having lost their conscious humanity. Conversely, those who give up anger are equal to the great ascetics who have renounced all worldly desires. The wordplay on the words meaning 'transgressed/died' and 'gave up/renounced' beautifully highlights how overcoming anger is equivalent to the highest spiritual renunciation.
